newsitem.title: UK: Dlr/mark elbows dlr/yen out of spotlight in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark elbows dlr/yen out of spotlight in Europe.

text.p: The dollar wound up European trading around a pfennig down on the day after new German data surprised the market with their strength.
German industrial production rose 1.9 percent month-on-month in February for a year-on-year jump of 7.1 percent, igniting a mark rally which was fuelled by 6.2 percent
The small print showed a seasonal rebound in construction was a big factor in the industrial output jump, while East Germany was the engine of growth in orders, Collins noted.
The dollar was quoted at 1.6656/66 marks at 1521 GMT, at session lows and down from late Wednesday's European level of 1.6755/65.
Its performance against the mark upstaged dollar/yen, which had been in the spotlight recently as it fell on concerns over trade tensions between the U.S. and Japan.
Dollar/yen stood at 122.61/66, just a touch down from its previous close here around 122.77/82.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin holds talks with Japan's prime minister and finance minister in Tokyo on Friday, having already spooked dollar/yen by warning Japan not to let its huge trade surplus swell again.
But he vehemently denied he was trying to trigger currency movements, and analysts said the market is now calmer about the outcome of the meetings.

"Expectations of a heavy-handed approach by Rubin...are looking likely to be disappointed, particularly in reference to exchange rates," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered in London.
For its part, Japan said it will tell Rubin it aims for growth centred on domestic demand, and that it does not see its trade surplus growing as rapidly as in the past.

Dollar/yen was unsettled in early Europe after the International Monetary Fund said some of the yen's depreciation could be reversed and the Matsushita Electric Industrial Co said it would be comfortable with the dollar around 110 yen.

But analysts said problems in the Japanese financial sector meant the Bank of Japan was unlikely to tighten credit soon -- meaning Japanese assets would remain unattractive on the basis of yield-differentials.

The market is on the alert for more U.S. tightening after last week's quarter-point Fed funds rate rise. Federal Reserve Board Vice Chairman Alice Rivlin said today the U.S. economy did not slow down as expected in the first quarter.
The economy was growing quite strongly and the risks for inflation were on the upside, Rivlin told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.

The market is now keenly awaiting Friday's U.S. non-farm payrolls data for March as a key gauge of economic health. Figures out today showed weekly jobless claims rose to 314,000 from 313,000 -- revised from 310,000 -- in the previous week.

A Reuters poll of economists predicts payrolls to have risen 182,000 after February's hefty 339,000 increase. Unemployment is seen easing to 5.2 percent from 5.3 but average hourly earnings growth is expected to tick up to 0.4 percent from 0.2 last time.

On the crosses, the mark firmed in early trade after the German data but pulled back after German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said he planned to stand for re-election in 1998 and reasserted that EU economic and monetary union would be launched punctually in 1999, with Germany meeting the entry criteria.
